topic: The Fundamental Bridge: The Relationship Between Integrals and Derivatives

outline.topic: The Fundamental Bridge: The Relationship Between Integrals and Derivatives

sections.title: Intuitive Hook: The Velocity-Distance Analogy
sections.content: Introduce the concept of motion. If you have a car's speedometer (derivative), you can track its position (integral). Define the derivative as the rate of change and the integral as the accumulation of change.
sections.example: A cheetah chasing a gazelle: The speedometer displays the 'derivative' of its position. As time passes, the 'area' under the speedometer graph represents the total distance the cheetah has covered.

sections.title: Visualizing the Inverse Operation
sections.content: Use a graphical animation: Show a slope tangent line sliding along a curve (derivative) and then show the same area filling up under that curve (integral). Explain that they are inverse processes, like multiplication and division.
sections.example: Visual animation: A 'Slope-O-Meter' showing how steep a mountain is at any point vs. a 'Rain Gauge' showing how much water has collected in a reservoir based on rainfall intensity.

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1)
sections.content: Formally connect the two: If F'(x) = f(x), then the integral of f(x) from a to b is F(b) - F(a). This shows that the accumulation of a rate of change equals the total net change.
sections.example: A robotic arm moving along a track: The robot's motor speed is f(x). By integrating the speed, we find the net change in the arm's position, which is simply the difference between the start and end coordinates.

sections.title: Synthesis and Summary
sections.content: Consolidate the concept: Derivative = Slope/Rate; Integral = Area/Accumulation. The Fundamental Theorem acts as the bridge connecting these two distinct geometric interpretations.
sections.example: A summary chart showing: [Function] -> [Derivative (Tangent Slope)] -> [Integral (Area under curve)]. The reverse path demonstrates the 'inverse' nature of these mathematical tools.

Integrals measure the accumulation of change.

Distance is the total area accumulated.

Integrals find the area under a curve.

Integrating the rate gives net change.
It equals final position minus initial.

Show moving vertical line at x, color #FFFFFF.
Visualize area accumulating as x moves right.
